problem_type: The coding-command secret-store rule misses Windows and quote-split spellings of the same credential file
symptom: On Windows the agent's bash tool asks for approval on every command (no OS sandbox). `cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` is denied outright by the hard list, but `cat "C:\Users\<name>\.ssh\id_ed25519"`, `type %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\id_rsa`, `cat ~/.s'sh'/id_rsa` and the Windows Nomi settings directory (`%APPDATA%\nomi`) fall through to an ordinary approval card; one click on it sends the key file into the conversation and to the model provider. Separately, `cat /usr/share/dict/words` is classified as outside-project on Windows.
direct_cause: SECRET_PATH_FRAGMENTS only lists POSIX spellings (`/.ssh`, `application support/nomi`) and buildSecretPattern matches them literally against the raw command, so backslashes, drive letters, env-var homes and quote-split fragments never match; the Nomi settings directory on Windows and Linux is not listed at all. isSystemReadOnly resolves POSIX prefixes with the host path.resolve, which prepends the drive on Windows (`/usr` → `C:\usr`).
class_root: Security and path rules were written against one platform's spelling and fed through host path semantics. On macOS a second layer (sandbox-runtime denyRead) hides the gap; on Windows there is no OS sandbox, so the hard list is the only layer that denies credential reads outright. Same class as 2026-09-24-lane-identity-host-path (a POSIX identity passed through host path.resolve).
affected_population: Windows users who use the agent's bash tool (coding tool group, skills with scripts): credential reads written with backslashes, drive letters, %USERPROFILE%/$USERPROFILE or quote-split names reach an approval card instead of being denied
Windows and Linux users: reads of the Nomi settings directory (%APPDATA%\nomi, ~/.config/nomi) were never on the list
macOS users with quote-split or escaped spellings (`~/.s'sh'`, `~/\.ssh`): caught by the OS sandbox today, now also by the hard list
entry_points: classifyCommand (the only verdict for every bash tool call, via laneNativeApproval)

external_sources.purpose: Bash removes quotes and backslash escapes before running a word, so `~/.s'sh'/id_rsa` and `~/\.ssh/id_rsa` name the same file as `~/.ssh/id_rsa`; the matching view must drop them too.
path.resolve on Windows prepends the current drive to a root-relative path; POSIX prefix tables must be compared with path.posix.
userData is %APPDATA%\<app name> on Windows and ~/.config/<app name> on Linux, i.e. the Nomi settings directory the secret-store rule must cover on those platforms.

invariants: Every spelling of a credential path that bash would resolve to the same file is denied by the hard list, with or without a sandbox
Normalization only widens what the hard list matches; the command that runs is never rewritten
POSIX path tables are compared with POSIX semantics on every host

invariant_owner_layer.why: classifyCommand is the single verdict for every bash call (laneNativeApproval is its only caller); the hard list is matched there against both the raw command and one normalized view (hardListView), so every caller gets the same answer.

door_reduction.why_not: One definition (codingCommandPolicy.ts) and one caller (laneNativeApproval.ts); there is nothing to merge.

generality_proof: The hard list is evaluated once per command in classifyCommand against the raw text and a view with quotes removed and backslash runs turned into '/', so a credential path is caught regardless of Windows separators, drive letters, env-var home prefixes or bash quote splitting; the secret pattern additionally names the Nomi settings directory in its Windows ($APPDATA, %APPDATA%, AppData/Roaming) and Linux (~/.config) forms.

shared_boundaries.responsibility: The one normalized spelling the hard list is compared against; never used to rewrite the executed command.

same_class_entry_points.evidence: POSIX prefixes are now resolved with path.posix; `cat /usr/share/dict/words` classifies the same on Windows as on macOS (the sample was red on Windows before).
Only reached when the sandbox is active (step ③ returns first otherwise), which never happens on Windows today; recorded as a residual risk for the day a Windows sandbox is enabled.
POSIX paths (`/tmp`, `~/.ssh`) in the sandbox policy only matter when the Windows sandbox is provisioned, which Nomi does not do; residual risk.

recurrence.reason: Any Windows user of the bash tool meets it whenever the model spells a home path the Windows way; every new secret path added in POSIX form would repeat it without the shared view.
same_class_scan: rg 'path.resolve' electron/shared/agentCapabilities: isSystemReadOnly and isInsideProject; only isSystemReadOnly compares against a POSIX table
Windows triage of tests/agent-runtime under Electron's Node (19 red cases classified; B1 is this contract)

prevention.invariant: The hard list matches every bash spelling of a protected path; POSIX tables are compared with POSIX semantics
prevention.failure_mode: A new spelling that bash resolves but the view does not normalize (globs, variables expanded at runtime) still reaches an approval card on Windows, never auto-allow: without a sandbox every non-hard-list command asks.
prevention.strategy: Compare the hard list against the raw command and one normalized view in the single verdict function; name the settings directory on every platform; test each spelling under both sandbox states.

legacy_paths.rationale: The rule is widened in place; there was no second matcher to remove.

dependency_lifecycle.rationale: Pure function in Nomi code; no third-party runtime involved.

migration: None. Remembered session grants are unaffected: on Windows none exist (grantable is false without a sandbox), and on macOS a grant never reaches past the hard list.
residual_risks: Glob and runtime-variable spellings (`~/.ss?/id*`, `$(echo ~)/.ssh`) are not normalized; on Windows they still land on an approval card showing the command, never auto-allow. macOS keeps the sandbox denyRead layer.
If a user provisions the Windows sandbox manually, laneCodingSandbox.mts policy paths and extractAbsolutePaths are POSIX-only; tracked from the Windows triage (C1).
Other credential files not on the list on any platform (e.g. ~/.git-credentials, gh hosts.yml) are a coverage question, not this spelling class.
